procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 23, 1965 of the Madhya Pradesh High Court (Indore Bench) in Criminal Revision No. 131 of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants moved the High Court of Madhya Pradesh in Criminal Revision No. 131 of 1964 to set aside their conviction. The High Court dismissed the revision on December 23, 1965.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's order confirming their conviction.

issue.issue_text: Whether there is evidence of any conspiracy to attract Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: A very large quantity of opium (about 2 maunds, 14 seers and 14 chhatacks) was recovered from the courtyard of the house where the appellants lived.
The trial court, the Sessions Judge, and the High Court had all previously found that the appellants had conspired to possess this opium.
The appellants argued that they lived separately and that an outsider could have thrown the opium into the courtyard.
law: Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code pertains to the punishment for criminal conspiracy.
A finding of conspiracy can be based on circumstantial evidence.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the concurrent findings of the three lower courts.

The Court noted that the lower courts had considered and rejected the appellants' defense, finding that the courtyard was a place in frequent use by the appellants and eliminating the chance of an outsider having thrown the opium there.

The Supreme Court endorsed the lower courts' reasoning that the presence of such a large quantity of opium would not have been possible without each of the appellants taking the others into their confidence.
This act of taking each other into confidence to obtain, deal in, and possess the opium was deemed to constitute the conspiracy.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no legal error or infirmity in the lower courts' conclusion. It upheld their finding that the appellants had conspired together and therefore rejected the contention that there was no evidence of a conspiracy under Section 120B of the IPC.

issue.issue_text: Whether the lower courts failed to consider the vital question of whether the evidence establishes that the appellants were in conscious possession of the opium recovered from the house.

facts: The appellants contended that the lower courts and the High Court failed to consider the vital question of whether the evidence established they were in 'conscious possession' of the opium.
The appellants' defense was that they lived separately, were not present when the opium was recovered, and that an outsider could have thrown the opium into their courtyard.
application: The Supreme Court found that, contrary to the appellants' claim, the lower courts (the Magistrate and the Sessions Judge) had explicitly considered the question of conscious possession.
In addressing this question, the lower courts had considered and rejected all of the appellants' specific pleas.

The lower courts made several key findings: the possibility of an outsider throwing the opium into the courtyard was eliminated; the courtyard was a place in frequent use by the appellants; and the appellants' presence at the time of the recovery was established.
Based on these circumstances, the lower courts recorded a specific finding that the opium was in the appellants' conscious possession.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the lower courts had properly considered the issue of conscious possession and that there was no legal error or infirmity in their conclusion. Therefore, the Court rejected the appellants' contention.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial was vitiated as it was held under Section 251A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, when it should have been held under Section 252.

facts: The investigation, seizure of articles, and arrest of the accused were all carried out by a police officer.
The report that initiated the trial before the Magistrate was made and signed by a Sub-Inspector of Police.

The appellants contended that under the special provisions of the Opium (Madhya Pradesh) Amendment Act, the police officer should be considered an excise officer, and his report was not a 'police report' within the meaning of Section 251A.
law: Section 251A of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) prescribes the trial procedure for cases instituted on a police report.
Section 252 of the Cr.P.C. prescribes the trial procedure for cases instituted otherwise than on a police report.

The Court referred to its previous decision in Amalshah's Case, which held that a trial for an offence under the Opium Act, when initiated on a report by a police officer, is correctly governed by Section 251A Cr.P.C.
application: The Court determined that the decisive factor was who actually made the report that initiated the trial.
In this case, the facts clearly showed that a police officer conducted the investigation and submitted the report to the Magistrate.
Because the proceedings commenced on a report made by a police officer, the Court found that Section 251A of the Cr.P.C. directly applied.
The Court explicitly chose not to decide the 'larger question' of whether a report made by an excise officer would also attract Section 251A, confining its ruling to the specific facts of the case.
Following its own precedent, the Court held that the procedure adopted for the trial was correct.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' contention, concluding that there was no illegality in the trial. Since the trial was initiated on a report made by a police officer, it was correctly held under the procedure prescribed by Section 251A of the Cr.P.C. and was therefore not vitiated.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there is evidence of any conspiracy to attract Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: There is no evidence of any conspiracy to attract Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code.
respondent_arguments: The appellants conspired together to obtain, deal in, and possess opium.
The presence of such a large quantity of opium would not have been possible without each of them taking the other into confidence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the lower courts failed to consider the vital question of whether the evidence establishes that the appellants were in conscious possession of the opium recovered from the house.
appellant_arguments: The High Court and the two subordinate courts failed to consider the vital question of whether the evidence establishes that the appellants were in conscious possession of the opium.
The appellants were living separately in the house, were not present at the time of recovery, and it was possible for an outsider to have thrown the opium into the courtyard.
respondent_arguments: The lower courts did consider the question of conscious possession.

The lower courts found that the courtyard was in frequent use by the appellants, their presence at the time of recovery was established, and the possibility of an outsider throwing the opium was eliminated, thus establishing conscious possession.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the trial was vitiated as it was held under Section 251A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, when it should have been held under Section 252.
appellant_arguments: The trial should have been held under Section 252 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.), not Section 251A.
Under the Opium (Madhya Pradesh) Amendment Act, the investigating police officer should be considered an excise officer.
Therefore, the report submitted by the officer is not a 'police report' within the meaning of Section 251A, making that procedure inapplicable.
respondent_arguments: The trial was correctly held under Section 251A Cr.P.C.
The case was investigated by a police officer and initiated on a report made by a police officer.
As the case was instituted on a police report, the procedure under Section 251A directly applies.

cases.case_name: Amalshah v. The State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.citation: Unreported decision in Crl. A. No. 201/63, dt. 11-12-64
cases.principle: In respect of a trial, conducted by a Magistrate, on a report made by a police officer, under the Opium Act, as applicable to the State of Madhya Pradesh, for an offence under that Act, s. 251-A, Cr.P.C. is applicable.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When an investigation is conducted by a police officer and the case is initiated on a report made by that police officer, the subsequent trial is governed by the procedure under Section 251A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and a trial held in accordance with that section is not illegal.
obiter: The court expressed no opinion on whether a trial would be governed by Section 251A of the Code of Criminal Procedure when a case is initiated on a report made by an excise officer.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appeal is dismissed because the appellants' contentions regarding conscious possession and conspiracy are merely an attack on the concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts, in which the Supreme Court finds no legal error or infirmity. Furthermore, the trial was not vitiated, as the procedure under Section 251A of the Cr.P.C. was correctly applied because the investigation was conducted and the report to the magistrate was made by a police officer, thus initiating the case on a police report.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a case was instituted on a 'police report' to determine the applicability of Section 251A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Standard of review for concurrent findings of fact by lower courts, which will not be overturned in the absence of a legal error or infirmity.
why_appellant_lost: The arguments against the findings of conspiracy and conscious possession were rejected as an impermissible attack on the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the Magistrate, the Sessions Judge, and accepted by the High Court.

The lower courts did, in fact, consider the question of conscious possession and recorded detailed findings against the appellants, eliminating the possibility of an outsider planting the opium and establishing that the courtyard was in frequent use by the appellants.

The trial was not vitiated because the investigation, seizure, and report to the Magistrate were all made by a police officer, meaning the case was instituted on a police report, which directly triggers the application of the procedure under Section 251A Cr.P.C.
why_respondent_won: The lower courts' findings, which were upheld, established that the opium was in the appellants' conscious possession and that the presence of such a large quantity could not have been possible without each of them taking the other into confidence, thus proving conspiracy.

The case was factually initiated on a report made by a police officer after an investigation by a police officer, which is the precise scenario for which the trial procedure under Section 251A Cr.P.C. is prescribed.
policy_considerations: The court demonstrated judicial restraint by confining its decision to the specific facts of the case, explicitly declining to express an opinion on the larger question of whether a report by an excise officer would also trigger the procedure under Section 251A Cr.P.C.
